query: For structural materials intended for fusion plasma-facing components, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs high-temperature plastic strain and toughness, and why? Specify a controlled comparison that would isolate the hypothesized cause, the observations predicted relative to an unperturbed baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In tungsten refractory high‐entropy alloys for fusion plasma‐facing components, the introduction of stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitates (SCCPs) governs high‐temperature plastic strain and toughness by providing coherent interfaces that promote dislocation transmission and minimize stress concentrations, thereby delaying premature crack initiation.
generation.material_initial_state: A tungsten refractory high-entropy alloy produced by conventional methods that lacks controlled, coherent nanoprecipitate formation (or contains incoherent precipitates).
generation.intervention: Modify processing to induce SCCPs via a tailored alloy design and heat-treatment protocol that produces nanoprecipitates with coherent interfaces.
generation.conditions: High-temperature mechanical testing (e.g., at 800 °C and above) under tensile and creep loading conditions, with all other alloy variables controlled so that the presence or absence of SCCPs is the primary difference.
generation.structural_mediator: Coherent nanoprecipitates with ideal interparticle spacing that interact favorably with dislocations.
generation.mechanism: The coherent interfaces of nanoprecipitates facilitate dislocation transmission across the matrix, concurrently reducing local stress concentrations that normally accelerate crack initiation. This dual effect promotes more uniform plastic strain and thus improves toughness at elevated temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline, the SCCP-treated alloy will exhibit higher high-temperature ductility, an increased capacity for plastic strain, and improved toughness, with observable differences in dislocation activity (e.g., more efficient dislocation motion and fewer stress concentrators) under identical loading conditions.
generation.baseline: An alloy with similar composition and microstructure except that it either lacks nanoprecipitates or contains incoherent precipitates that do not facilitate dislocation movement.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold in tungsten refractory high-entropy alloys under high-temperature conditions typical for fusion plasma-facing component applications (around 800 °C and higher) where the microstructural control of precipitate coherence is achievable.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement in ductility and toughness and the sensitivity of the effect to precipitate size, spacing, and degree of coherence remain uncertain. Interactions with other microstructural features not isolated in this comparison may also influence the outcome.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of tungsten refractory high-entropy alloy samples: one set processed to generate stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitates (SCCPs) and a control set processed without this intervention (resulting in either no precipitates or incoherent precipitates). Subject both sets to identical high-temperature tensile and creep tests (e.g., at 800 °C) while performing in-depth microstructural characterization (TEM/SEM) to confirm the presence or absence and coherence of the nanoprecipitates.
measurements: Stress-strain curves from high-temperature tensile tests
Creep rate measurements under constant stress
Dislocation motion and fracture analysis via TEM/SEM
Quantitative analysis of precipitate size, spacing, and interface coherence
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the SCCP-treated samples do not show a statistically significant increase in plastic strain and toughness (i.e., improved ductility, lower stress concentrations, and delayed crack initiation) compared to the baseline samples, or if microstructural examination reveals no difference in dislocation behavior correlated with coherent precipitates, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract High-performance refractory alloys with ultrahigh strength and ductility are in demand for a wide range of critical applications, such as plasma-facing components. However, it remains challenging to increase the strength of these alloys without seriously compromising their tensile ductility. Here, we put forward a strategy to “defeat” this trade-off in tungsten refractory high-entropy alloys by stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations (SCCPs). The coherent interfaces of SCCPs facilitate the dislocation transmission and relieve the stress concentrations that can lead to premature crack initiation. As a consequence, our alloy displays an ultrahigh strength of 2.15 GPa with a tensile ductility of 15% at ambient temperature, with a high yield strength of 1.05 GPa at 800 °C. The SCCPs design concept may afford a means to develop a wide range of ultrahigh-strength metallic materials by providing a pathway for alloy design. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Mechanical engineering

Materials with high performance both at room and elevated temperatures are very attractive for a wide range of critical applications, potentially for aero-engine and fusion reactors [1] – [4] . For decades, ultra-strong, ductile, and heat-resistant materials have long been sought by the materials community, such as tungsten-based heavy alloys and nickel-based superalloys [3] , [5] . However, achieving alloys with an ultrahigh strength (>2 GPa) and a sufficient ductility (>10%) has presented a long-standing challenge. This has spurred significant research into metallurgical strategies to tailor microstructures for improved properties. One classical design paradigm is utilizing dilute concentrations of alloying elements, such as Re, Ti, and Cr, to improve the properties of W-based alloys; however, the “strength-ductility trade-off” has proven to be difficult to be solved with such single principal-element alloy systems due to the problem of brittle W-enriched phases with body-centered cubic (bcc) structures [5] , [6] .
